title: Ukraine can do more to counter Russia’s illicit finance threat
gist: Russia treats finance as a stand-alone national security domain and uses illicit flows (payments to saboteurs, money mules, illegal exchange houses, crypto) inside Ukraine; Kyiv's anti-money-laundering architecture is still built around domestic corruption rather than countering Russian illicit finance as a security threat.

insights.claim: Russia's official defense doctrine treats finance both as part of its non-kinetic toolkit and as a stand-alone national security domain.
insights.speaker: Peter Dickinson
insights.so_what: Expect Russian hybrid operations to keep running through financial channels; compliance and sanctions exposure extends beyond the battlefield.
insights.quote: Russia’s official defense doctrine treats finance as both part of its non-kinetic toolkit and a stand-alone national security domain.
insights.locator: Russia’s official defense doctrine treats finance

insights.claim: In Ukraine, Russian illicit finance shows up as payments to saboteurs, exploitation of money mules, and illegal exchange houses used to move money out of Russia.
insights.speaker: Peter Dickinson
insights.so_what: Payment processors and exchanges in the region face elevated AML/CFT scrutiny tied to sabotage financing.
insights.locator: Russia’s official defense doctrine treats finance

insights.claim: Crypto currencies underpin much of Russia's sabotage effort in Ukraine, while Ukraine's legislation still relies on powers designed to prevent physical forgeries.
insights.speaker: Peter Dickinson
insights.so_what: Crypto rails used for state-sponsored sabotage are a regulatory catalyst for tighter virtual-asset rules in Ukraine and the EU.
insights.quote: the twenty-first century threat of crypto currencies, which underpins so much of Russia’s sabotage efforts

themes.theme: Ukraine's crypto law and institutional gaps

insights.claim: Ukraine is considering a draft law to create a legal and tax framework for virtual assets and crypto, which would raise tax revenue, align with EU standards, and give a basis to counter Russian weaponisation of crypto markets.
insights.speaker: Peter Dickinson
insights.so_what: Passage would formalise a regulated crypto market in Ukraine — watch for licensing opportunities for compliant exchanges and tighter KYC.
insights.locator: A draft law is currently under consideration

insights.claim: Ukraine's anti-corruption agencies NABU and SAPO, built since 2014, remain focused on domestic corruption rather than on illicit finance tied to Russia's invasion, leaving the issue to fall between agencies.
insights.speaker: Peter Dickinson
insights.so_what: Institutional gap implies continued leakage of sabotage finance until a unified strategy emerges.
insights.locator: Ukraine’s operational response has much in common

insights.claim: The SBU security service has counter-intelligence responsibility but lacks the institutional toolkit to tackle financial crimes the way other Ukrainian agencies can; the author calls for inter-agency cooperation and a unified national strategy.
insights.speaker: Peter Dickinson
insights.so_what: Watch for SBU financial-intelligence mandates as a signal of Ukraine treating illicit finance as security.

insights.claim: Western partners have focused on building Ukraine's anti-corruption architecture rather than a systemic response to Russian financial threats; cooperation would give allies insight into Russian illicit finance techniques they also face.
insights.speaker: Peter Dickinson
insights.so_what: Allied AML regimes may borrow Ukrainian typologies — relevant for European banks' Russia-related sanctions compliance.

insights.claim: Kyiv could adopt an offensive stance on illicit finance, including options to degrade nodes of the Russian financial system upstream.
insights.speaker: Peter Dickinson
insights.so_what: Potential for Ukrainian-led disruption (cyber or legal) of Russian payment nodes — a tail risk for counterparties touching those nodes.
insights.locator: In common with every other aspect

insights.claim: The core debate is whether Ukraine and partners frame illicit finance as a national security threat rather than as a domestic anti-corruption issue or an EU accession box-ticking item.
insights.speaker: Peter Dickinson
insights.so_what: Reframing as security would unlock different tools (intelligence, sanctions) than accession-driven compliance.
insights.locator: Ukraine’s state institutions have certainly not been idle
